sections.html:
Eddy County occupies New Mexico's southeast corner, up against Texas. Carlsbad is the county seat, Artesia is the other city, and Hope and Loving are villages. The 2020 census counted 62,314 residents: 32,238 in Carlsbad, 12,875 in Artesia, 1,390 in Loving and 15,811 in the rest of the county.

About a quarter of residents live outside any incorporated place, and a rural house is taxed by a different mix of districts than one inside Carlsbad or Artesia. Oil and gas, potash, the federal Waste Isolation Pilot Plant and tourism drive local jobs, so housing demand can swing with drilling and plant schedules. Workers on short assignments often rent, which is why many Eddy County owners end up as landlords.

sections.h2: Who values property and who collects
sections.html:
The Eddy County Assessor values property. The Eddy County Treasurer bills and collects. Under state law the county assessor does the valuing, with these exceptions: railroads, pipelines, utilities, airlines, power plants and mineral property, all valued by the state Taxation and Revenue Department. In oil country that carve-out is big: 531 properties statewide, worth $32 billion and about 17 percent of the tax base, are valued by the state.

OfficeWhat it doesAddress or phone
Eddy County TreasurerSends bills, takes payments101 W. Greene St., Suite 117, Carlsbad, NM 88220; (575) 885-3913
Eddy County AssessorSets values, takes exemption claims and protests(575) 885-3813
Point and Pay portalOnline payment by bill searchLinked from the county site

Current hours are on the county's treasurer and assessor pages, worth a look before you drive over.

Your bill should arrive by November 1. Pay half by November 10 and half by April 10 of the next year. Interest waits until December 10 for the first half and May 10 for the second.

Property is valued as of January 1. The state fixes rates near September 1.

Unpaid property tax is no ordinary debt. Starting each January 1 it attaches to the real property as a first lien, outranking every other interest, recorded or not. Nobody has to file anything for it to exist, so a search of recorded documents will miss it. Ask the treasurer for today's balance before you list or accept an offer.

sections.h2: How valuation works and what changes at sale
sections.html:
As long as one owner keeps a home, its taxable residential value climbs by at most 3 percent a year. The exact ceiling is whichever is higher: 103 percent of last year's figure, or 106.1 percent of the figure from two years ago. A sale resets it, as do a first valuation year, new improvements and a change of use or zoning.

One third of assessed value is taxable, and rates are set only after yield control adjusts them.

In practice, the buyer's first-year value is reset to current market value, so the new owner may pay more than you did. After decades of ownership, expect questions about that jump. The $2,000 head of family exemption protects a resident's primary home and falls away on a sale, which means the buyer has to claim it again.

  • A transfer to your spouse, or to a child living in the home, is one of the listed exceptions to "change of ownership."
  • Moving the house into a revocable trust for yourself, a spouse or a child is excepted as well.
  • Deeding the house to an LLC you own does count as a change of ownership, a New Mexico Court of Appeals decision held.

Write out your protest and deliver it to the county assessor. The deadline is April 1 or 30 days after the notice of valuation was mailed, whichever is later. The county valuation protest board decides it, and a state Taxation and Revenue appraiser holds one of its seats.

Filing on time keeps the disputed portion from going delinquent. The alternative is paying up front and asking district court for a refund by January 10 of the next year.

The state's protest pamphlet lists the statute citations.

Interest begins once the December 10 and May 10 dates pass. When a third full year of delinquency ends, the state takes over the account. Its Delinquent Property Tax Bureau tries phone calls, certified letters, visits to the property and posted notices, and it will set up installment agreements. Public auction is the last resort, and every county must hold one each calendar year.

An auction pays off the tax, penalty, interest and costs first, and whatever is left goes to the former owner. That is a poor way to part with a house you could have sold.

  • An inherited home may still get bills addressed to the person who died.
  • Absentee owners of rural parcels can miss notices that go to an old address.

Pull together three things: the treasurer's balance, the assessor's record of who holds the land and the minerals, and the clerk's recorded documents. An unrecorded deed or mortgage does not bind a later purchaser in New Mexico, so recording is not optional.

Insist that offers come in writing, learn who covers recording and title costs, and compare the figure to your payoff and tax due.

A cash sale has no lender appraisal or underwriting in the way, so timing depends on how fast the title company clears the lien and records the deed. Keep the tax balance and a copy of your deed handy. If you hold mineral rights, tell the title company early, since the land and the minerals may have different owners of record.

sections.h2: A plan for selling in Eddy County
sections.html:
Listing with an agent or selling for cash, you do the same groundwork whether the house is in Carlsbad, Artesia or out in the country.

  1. Call the treasurer at (575) 885-3913 and request the balance for each year. Years in delinquency are the ones that can reach the state.
  2. Ring the assessor at (575) 885-3813 to learn if the head of family exemption sits on your account and if any protest is still open.
  3. Check who is named as owner of the land and of any minerals, and make sure your deed is recorded.
  4. Hand the payoff figures to the title company. It will settle the lien from your proceeds and deliver clean title.
  5. Warn the buyer that the exemption ends at sale, which makes the first bill under new ownership look different.

Owners who rented the house to workers on short assignments should also gather lease papers and tell the buyer about any tenant who is staying.

faqs.q: When is Eddy County property tax due?
faqs.a: Half comes due November 10 and the rest April 10. You have until December 10 and May 10, respectively, before interest starts.

faqs.q: Who do I call about my Eddy County property tax bill?
faqs.a: The Eddy County Treasurer, at (575) 885-3913, handles bills and payments from 101 W. Greene St., Suite 117, in Carlsbad. Call the Assessor at (575) 885-3813 for valuations and exemptions.

faqs.q: How much can my Eddy County home value increase each year?
faqs.a: The limit is the higher of 103 percent of last year's value or 106.1 percent of the figure from two years back. When ownership changes, the limit resets.

faqs.q: Is there a New Mexico estate or inheritance tax on an Eddy County house?
faqs.a: No. The state's estate tax ended as of January 1, 2005, and there is no inheritance tax. Only very large estates can still owe federal estate tax.

faqs.q: Can I sell an Eddy County house with property tax owed?
faqs.a: Yes, but the lien dates from January 1 and outranks other interests, so it must be paid or settled before the buyer gets clean title. Start with a payoff from the treasurer.
